confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gedney, William J. 1989 [1964]. A comparative sketch of White, Black and Red Tai. In R. J. Bickner, J. Hartmann, T. J. Hudak & P. Peyasantiwong (eds.), Selected papers on comparative Tai studies (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 29), 415-461. Ann Arbor: Center for South and Southeast Asian Studies, University of Michigan. [orig. Social Science Review (Bangkok), special number, 14 December 1964: 1-47]
catalog_locator: p. 421, second-to-last paragraph before the heading COMPARISON OF TONES. Supporting: p. 418 syllable statement; p. 420 'Black Tai, like White Tai, has six tones' and 'On checked syllables Black Tai has'.
catalog_quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. Though this phenomenon would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language, it is so infrequent in the type of words that we are dealing with that we can get along by the simple device of placing a short mark ˘ over the vowel; if we know from slower pronunciation what the reduced tone would have been, we will mark it, for example S măphraaw4 or mă4phraaw4 'coconut.' It is noteworthy that of the four languages here studied, Siamese has by far the greatest number of such weak syllables, Red Tai somewhat fewer, Black Tai still fewer, and in White Tai they are infrequent. This order coincides with the relative geographical location of the languages.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tai Dam (Black Tai) is a tone language of essentially monosyllabic words (five/six lexical tones on 'normal' syllables). The only stress phenomenon described is that a minority of words contain a weakly stressed presyllable (typically short a, tone neutralised to mid level) prefixed to a fully stressed normal syllable; such sesquisyllables are rare in Black Tai. No word-stress rule or stress contrast is stated for ordinary (monosyllabic) words; prominence in the presyllable+main-syllable words falls on the final, full syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author notes the phenomenon is infrequent in Black Tai and would need a more thorough analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (presyllable + normal syllable within a word); citation forms from elicitation with Black Tai refugees from the Son La area (1964). Nothing on phrase-level stress. Diguet 1895 (p.31) independently confirms the monosyllabic-tonal picture for Black Tai without any accent statement; CAL 1975 (p.7) likewise says only that Black Tai is a tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: Gedney's 'Black Tai' data (the quoted source) come from Tai Dam speakers of the Son La area of northwest Vietnam interviewed as refugees in South Vietnam and Vientiane in 1964, i.e. taid1247 proper (Diguet 1895 likewise describes the Black Tai of the Black River, Tonkin). This is distinct from Thai Song / Lao Song of central Thailand (Glottolog thai1259, ISO soa), which has its own folder in this compilation; the Anuntrawan 1978 thesis describes a Tai Dam migrant community in Loei, Thailand, and Pheuaphom 2024 the Tai Dam of Xieng Khouang, Laos.

tone_statements.quote: In regards to speech tone, this paper will follow the results of William Gedney [3], who found six tones in the Tai Dam language: low-mid level, high rising, low falling, high level, higher-mid level and mid-falling. These tones are confirmed by several authors such as Hartmann [4] and Fippinger [2]. ... A first analysis of a khap Tai Dam from Laos and its spoken version seems to confirm the six tones developed by Gedney (although, Gedney’s observations on the glottalization of tone 3 were not observed in the analysis realised for this paper).

tone_statements.quote: While the 1-5 numerals designate the phonetic values of tones, tone numbers (tone 1- tone 6) are assigned to contrastive tones. Thai Song at all locations, except at Loei (Ananthrawan 1978), have six tones. The tone numbers in some studies were adjusted so that their tone numbers conformed to most studies, that is, tone 1 (A123), tone 2 (A4), tone 3 (B123), tone 4 (B4), tone 5 (C123), and tone 6 (C4) as seen in Diagram 2. The Loei variety has five tones, so C123 tones were labeled as tone 4 and C4 as tone 5.

"The Modern Black Tai tone system is a straightforward case of a binary register split. The second-series tones A2 (=tone 4), B2 (= tone 5), and C2 (=tone 6) can be viewed as a higher version of the first-series tones A1 (= tone 1), B1 (= tone 2), and C1 (= tone 3) respectively. As tones A1 and A2 are all level tones, we can posit a level tone for the original Black Tai system. Similarly, both C1 and C2 are glottalized falling tones, indicating that Black Tai *C must have been a glottalized falling tone. In the case of *B, tone B2 can be considered tone B1 with a raised onset resulting from the register split. Therefore, we can reconstruct Black Tai *B as a rising tone. Therefore, Black Tai *A, *B, and *C were a mid, a rising, and a falling tone, respectively. Notice that both *DL and *DS are tied to *B." tone_statements.citation: Hartmann, John F. (1992). Tai Dam poetics and Proto-Tai tone categories. In Papers on Tai languages, Linguistics, and Literatures. Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Northern Illinois University. pp. 262-277.
tone_statements.quote: To recapitulate the history of the changes from the four proto-Tai tone categories to their bifurcation into six modern Tai Dam tones, the original tones underwent a simple splitting along the lines of proto-voiceless and proto-voiced initial consonants. An identical two-way split affected neighboring White Tai (Tai Don) and Tai Lue. [...] The six modern Tai Dam tones have been described as follows: 1. lower mid-level 2. high-rising 3. low/low rising, glottalized 4. high-level 5. high mid-level 6. mid-falling, glottalized [...] In the system we have adopted for numbering modern Tai Dam tones, 1 and 4 = *A; 2 and 5 = *B; 3 and 6 = *C. The D category (tones 2 and 5) turns out to be similar to the B (2 and 5).

sources.quote: Of interest is the fact that most of the rhymes fall into Proto-Tai tone categories. That is, modern Tai Dam tones 1 and 4 =*A; 2 and 5 = *B; 3 and 6 = *C, an underlying phenomenon first pointed out by Gedney (1978).
sources.locator: printed p. 199, Appendix; also printed p. 187: 'In older texts, tonal rhymes based on Proto-Tai tone categories (A, B, C, D) can also be shown.'
sources.note: A pronoun study of a Tai Dam (Black Tai) poetic text, not a phonological description. Tone is mentioned only in passing: forms are transcribed with tone numerals 1-6 (khun1 terng4, taaw6, naang4, sau1/sau2), and the appendix maps the six modern Tai Dam tones onto Proto-Tai *A/*B/*C (1,4=*A; 2,5=*B; 3,6=*C), credited to Gedney (1978). This confirms the catalog's lexical-tone class for Black Tai (cite Gedney 1989 [1964]) and adds a six-tone count for the author's Lao-Tai Dam (Iowa refugee) community. Nothing on word stress, secondary stress, weight or domain. No measurement.

sources.citation: Hartmann, John F. (1992). Tai Dam poetics and Proto-Tai tone categories. In Papers on Tai languages, Linguistics, and Literatures. Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Northern Illinois University. pp. 262-277.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: To recapitulate the history of the changes from the four proto-Tai tone categories to their bifurcation into six modern Tai Dam tones, the original tones underwent a simple splitting along the lines of proto-voiceless and proto-voiced initial consonants. An identical two-way split affected neighboring White Tai (Tai Don) and Tai Lue. [...] The six modern Tai Dam tones have been described as follows: 1. lower mid-level 2. high-rising 3. low/low rising, glottalized 4. high-level 5. high mid-level 6. mid-falling, glottalized [...] In the system we have adopted for numbering modern Tai Dam tones, 1 and 4 = *A; 2 and 5 = *B; 3 and 6 = *C. The D category (tones 2 and 5) turns out to be similar to the B (2 and 5).
sources.locator: printed pp. 262-264: proto-Tai tone chart and split statement p. 262, tone list 1-4 p. 263, tones 5-6 and the *A/*B/*C/*D mapping p. 264
sources.note: Confirms the catalog's classification tonal coding for Black Tai (taid1247; catalog source Gedney 1989 [1964], six tones). Hartmann gives six modern Tai Dam tones from a two-way (proto-voiceless/proto-voiced initial) split of the four proto-Tai categories *A *B *C *D, with checked syllables (*D) falling together with *B (tones 2 and 5); tone 3 and tone 6 are glottalized. The paper says nothing about word stress in Tai Dam (the only stress remark, p. 265, is about an unstressed short -a- presyllable in a Siamese raay line); no secondary stress, weight or domain statements. sources.quote: A more recent case of 'transplanted Lao', or actually Black Tai, is found in the Lao Song community near Chumphon, an offshoot of the larger captive Black Tai community resettled in Phetburi in the early 19th century. Chumphon Black Tai appears to be conservative with respect to its six-tone [H+M]/[L] tonal system but local Southern Thai is supplying many lexical items and introducing phonological innovations, such as aspirated stops with L-series tones. [note 5, pp. 339-340]
sources.note: Passing remark: six tones from a two-way [H+M]/[L] register split, matching the catalog's six-tone lexical-tone entry (Gedney). Nothing on stress. Author's own field observation of the Chumphon community, not a description.
